tracks.title: Describing data
tracks.summary: A short path from where a batch of numbers sits, through spread and skew, to pictures of outliers and of departure from a reference shape.

steps.title: Mean, Median, and Mode
steps.note: Start with three summaries of where a batch of numbers sits.

steps.title: Moments
steps.note: Treat the mean as the first moment, then use higher moments for spread and shape.

steps.title: Bessel's Correction
steps.note: See why the sample variance, that second moment, divides by n − 1 rather than n.

steps.title: Skewed Distribution
steps.note: Watch the mean, median, and mode pull apart when the distribution leans to one side.

steps.title: Boxplot and Histogram
steps.note: Read that shape two ways: a histogram of the values, and a boxplot of center and spread.

steps.title: Boxplot and Outliers
steps.note: See how the boxplot marks points that sit far from the rest of the data.

steps.title: Q-Q Plot
steps.note: Compare the sample's quantiles with a reference distribution, often the normal.

tracks.title: Statistical reasoning
tracks.summary: A short path from the shape of a normal curve, through sampling and the chi-square distribution, to what a confidence interval claims.

steps.title: Building the Normal Distribution
steps.note: See how a normal curve is assembled before treating it as a model for data.

steps.title: Central Limit Theorem (CLT)
steps.note: Watch sample means pile into that shape as each sample gets larger.

steps.title: Horowitz (1974) CLT Simulation
steps.note: Replay Horowitz's classroom simulation of the same sampling result.

steps.title: Chi-Square Distribution
steps.note: Square standard normal draws and add them to build a chi-square curve.

steps.title: Target Analogy of Confidence Intervals
steps.note: Sampling distributions set a coverage rate; see what that rate does and does not say about one interval.

tracks.title: t-test
tracks.summary: A short path from the t curve used when the population standard deviation is unknown to tests of two separate groups and of two paired measures.

steps.title: z-Distribution vs t-Distribution
steps.note: Compare the z curve with the heavier-tailed t curve used when the population standard deviation is unknown.

steps.title: Independent Samples t-Test
steps.note: Use that t curve to compare means from two separate groups.

steps.title: Paired Sample t-Test
steps.note: Compare two measures on the same people, so pairing removes a source of person-to-person noise.

tracks.title: Statistical power
tracks.summary: A short path from the chance of detecting a real effect to how that chance changes with the effect and the sample.

steps.title: Statistical Power
steps.note: Lay the sampling distribution under the alternative against the null, and see power as the share that falls past the cutoff.

steps.title: Power Curve
steps.note: Trace how that share grows as the effect or the sample gets larger.

tracks.title: ANOVA
tracks.summary: A short path from the two-group t-test to several means, a split of the variation, and the assumptions the F test needs.

steps.title: From t-Test to ANOVA
steps.note: See the two-group t-test as the special case of comparing more than two means.

steps.title: Partitioning Sum of Squares
steps.note: Split the total variation into a part between groups and a part left inside groups.

steps.title: Two-Way ANOVA
steps.note: Add a second factor, and separate each main effect from the interaction.

steps.title: ANOVA Assumptions
steps.note: Check the normality, equal spread, and independence the F test relies on.

tracks.title: Association
tracks.summary: A short path from how two variables move together, through the share of variance one accounts for, to the case where separate sources of variance add.

steps.title: Covariance and Correlation
steps.note: See covariance as shared movement, then scale it to a correlation free of the units.

steps.title: Variance Explained
steps.note: Square that correlation to get the share of variance one variable accounts for in the other.

steps.title: Additivity of Variance
steps.note: When sources of variance are independent, they do not overlap, and the total variance is their sum.
